The pressure inside the tank is measured by a gauge pressure sensor and maintained within +/- 2.1 kPa, which means the fluid is always boiling near the local atmospheric pressure and that its bulk temperature is kept at saturated boiling conditions. The tank has two separate mechanisms to maintain its pressure. When the gauge pressure is positive, a set of variable volume bags, called bellows, will inflate. If the gauge pressure continues to increase because of changes in operating conditions and reaches + 2.1 kPa, a venting valve will open into a cold trap until the gauge pressure is zero. The cold trap in this tank consists of a thermoelectric cold plate that typically operates around 10–15°C. If the gauge pressure is negative, the bellows will deflate. If the pressures continue to reduce and reaches -2.1 kPa, a vacuum breaker will open and admit air into the system to equalize the pressure. The system also has a buffer tank and a filtration loop with a small filter pump that circulates dielectric fluid from the buffer tank through an activated carbon filter before discharging back into the main tank. Under normal operating conditions, liquid will overflow from the main tank into the buffer tank, which maintains steady liquid levels. If vapor loss occurs, only the liquid level in the buffer tank will go down, while the main tank liquid level is kept constant as liquid overflows to the buffer tank. Changes in the buffer tank liquid level are captured by a liquid level sensor. Low-level alarms and safety cut-out for the buffer tank and the main tank are also present. Depending on the coolant temperatures and the heat load inside the tank, air concentrations will vary within the vapor space of the tank, between the liquid surface and the lid. Higher heat loads and coolant temperatures will increase concentration of dielectric fluid vapor and decrease the air concentration. Two temperature sensors are placed in the vapor space, as shown in Figure 1, one next to the first condenser tube from top to bottom—called “vapor high (T )”—and one next to the second tube—called “vapor vap,high mid (T ).” The T is positioned 0.15 m above the liquid surface, while the T is placed 0.11 m vap,mid vap,high vap,mid above the liquid surface. These sensors give an indirect relative indication of air concentration inside the 3 tank (i.e., the higher these temperatures the lower the air concentrations). The vapor high (T ) sensor vap,high also helps protect the system from insufficient cooling for a given heat load and coolant temperature. A vapor high temperature alarm, typically set at a few degrees below the fluid’s normal boiling point, will interrupt the heat load to avoid a significant loss of fluid vapor through the tank’s pressure relief device.
